911.title: The mango given at the door

911.carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is God

911.howItsDone: Karaikkal Ammaiyar is honored among the Nayanars in Shiva temples, and in Karaikkal a mango festival remembers the story of the two mangoes.

segments.voice: Two mangoes arrive at a merchant's house in the port town of Karaikkal. The merchant sent them home for his lunch. His wife, Punitavati, puts them aside. Then a knock: a wandering devotee of Shiva, worn out and hungry. She has rice but nothing to go with it, so she gives him rice and one of the mangoes. He eats, blesses her, and goes. Then her husband comes home, eats the remaining mango, loves it, and says: bring me the other one.
screen: `TWO MANGOES.` → `ONE GOES TO A HUNGRY GUEST.` → `BRING ME THE OTHER ONE.`

segments.voice: The Periya Puranam tells it like this. Punitavati goes into the kitchen and prays to Shiva, and a mango appears in her hand. It's so sweet her husband asks where it came from, and she tells him the truth. Then get me another, he says. She prays again, another mango appears, and the moment he takes it, it vanishes. Now he's afraid. Not angry: afraid. So he quietly sails away on business, settles in another town, marries again, and names his daughter Punitavati. Punitavati doesn't ask for him back. She asks Shiva to take away the beauty she kept for her husband and give her the form of a pey, a gaunt, ghost-like being. She sets out for Shiva's mountain and, the Periya Puranam says, goes up on her head, so her feet won't touch the holy ground. Shiva sees her coming and calls her Mother. She's Karaikkal Ammaiyar, the mother of Karaikkal. Now look at where it all began: a mango given to a hungry stranger. Not just any stranger: a devotee of Shiva. For the Nayanars, serving Shiva's devotees was serving Shiva himself. Behind it is an old Hindu teaching, in the Taittiriya Upanishad's words: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be God to you. It's why so many Hindu grandmothers won't let anyone leave unfed, and why the guest is so often served first. Punitavati fed the guest before her husband, and the story says Shiva himself filled her hand.
screen: `A MANGO APPEARS IN HER HAND.` · `HE SAILS AWAY, AFRAID.` · `SHIVA CALLS HER MOTHER.` · then, large: `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST IS GOD.`

segments.voice: Picture your front door, and someone knocking who needs something small. Notice the voice that says save it for later; just breathe beside it. If you don't pray, choose one person you'll serve first this week, before yourself.

912.title: The boy who answered with a song
912.hook: milk on a small boy's lips, and a father who wants to know who gave it
912.carry: for the saints, singing to God is worship
912.howItsDone: Tamil Shaivas sing hymns from the Tevaram in temple worship, often led by singers called oduvars, and the story of Sambandar and the milk is remembered at the Sirkazhi temple.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Nayanars again. Karaikkal Ammaiyar gave a mango to Shiva's devotee at her door: atithi devo bhava, the guest is God.

segments.voice: A father leaves his little boy on the steps of a temple tank and wades in to bathe, ducking under the water to say his prayers. On the steps, the boy can't see his father and starts to cry, calling for his mother and father, looking toward the temple tower. When the father comes up, the crying has stopped. The boy is calm. And there's milk on his lips. Nobody else is there.
screen: `A BOY ON THE TEMPLE STEPS.` → `HE CRIES FOR HIS PARENTS.` → `MILK ON HIS LIPS.`

segments.voice: The town is Sirkazhi, and the boy is known as Sambandar. In the Periya Puranam, when he cries, Shiva and Parvati come to the tank, and Parvati, the Mother of the world, feeds him milk from a golden cup. Then they're gone. His father, a careful Brahmin, sees the milk and is furious. Who fed you? Food from a stranger's hand could break the rules he lives by. He picks up a stick. And the small boy, instead of explaining, points up at the sky and sings. That song, as tradition remembers it, describes the one who wears an earring in his ear, who rides the bull, who wears the pale crescent moon, and then calls him the thief who stole my heart. The boy's answer to who fed you is: him. And his answer comes as a song. That's the heart of bhakti, loving devotion, as the Tamil saints lived it: you don't only think about God, you sing to him, and the singing itself is worship. Sambandar sang all his life, from temple to temple. His songs, with those of Appar and Sundarar, are gathered as the Tevaram, and in Tamil Shiva temples, singers called oduvars still sing them in worship. It's a big part of why so much Hindu devotion is sung: bhajans in living rooms, kirtan in temples. Kannappa offered with his hands, Karaikkal Ammaiyar at her door, Sambandar with his voice.
screen: `PARVATI'S CUP OF MILK.` · `WHO FED YOU?` · `HE POINTS UP AND SINGS.` · then, large: `THE SINGING IS THE WORSHIP.`

segments.voice: Choose a name of God you know, Shiva, Krishna, Ram, or simply Om, and sing it softly on one easy note, three times, the way many bhajans begin. It doesn't have to be good; a child's voice was enough. If you pray, let the singing be the prayer. If you don't, hum one note and listen to it, and think of someone who fed you when you thought you were alone.

segments.voice: Four children walk into a town of learned Brahmins with a request. Three brothers and a little sister, shut out by their community their whole lives, through no fault of their own. They want to be accepted. The scholars look them over and start to laugh. One points at a buffalo plodding by, and makes a joke about names. Today the path moves north and west, into the Marathi-speaking country, and meets the second of those children: Jnaneshwar.
screen: `FOUR CHILDREN, SHUT OUT.` → `THE SCHOLARS LAUGH.` → `A BUFFALO WALKS BY.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as tradition tells it. The children's father had left home to become a sannyasi, a renunciant. His teacher sent him back home. To their community, a monk who goes home has broken the order of things, and the family is cast out. Four children are born into that: Nivritti, Jnanadev, Sopan, and their sister Muktabai. Before long, the story says, they're on their own. So they go to the Brahmins of Paithan to ask for a letter of purification that would let them belong. Hearing the second boy's name, Jnanadev, which carries the Sanskrit word for knowledge, someone mocks him: names mean nothing; look, that buffalo has a name too. Jnaneshwar doesn't argue. The story says he answers that the same Self lives in the buffalo as in him, and places his hand on its head. And the buffalo begins to recite the Veda, the text these men spent their lives learning. The scholars fall silent, and some tellings say they then grant the letter. This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings, acted out in a street. The Upanishads call it atman: the Self, the deepest you, is one and the same in every being, a scholar, an outcast child, a buffalo. If that's true, the line between those worth hearing and those who don't count was never real. And the Varkari path that honors Jnaneshwar came to include saints who were a tailor, a potter, a maidservant, and Chokhamela, whose caste was treated as untouchable.
screen: `A MONK WHO WENT HOME.` · `THE BRAHMINS OF PAITHAN.` · `THE VEDA FROM AN ANIMAL'S MOUTH.` · then, large: `ATMAN: THE SAME SELF IN EVERY BEING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a creature you rarely think about, a pigeon, a stray dog, an insect, breathing too. Then add a person you tend to look past. Hold them both, and say quietly: the same Self in you as in me. If you pray, hold them before God in words you already use. If you don't, just let them both stay.

914.title: The Gita in the people's language
914.hook: the Gita, carried out of Sanskrit and into the language of the street
914.carry: God's word belongs in everyone's own tongue

914.howItsDone: Varkari devotees read the Jnaneshwari aloud in groups, at home and in temples, and many read it along the way on the pilgrimage to Pandharpur.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jnaneshwar, the outcast boy at Paithan whose buffalo recited the Veda. Atman: the same self lives in every being.
screen: `JNANESHWAR.` · `THE SAME SELF IN EVERY BEING.`

segments.voice: A temple in a small town by a river. A young man sits near a stone pillar and talks, verse by verse, through the Bhagavad Gita. Not in Sanskrit, the language of the priests, but in Marathi, the language of the farmers, the potters, the women at the well, the people sitting in front of him. Beside him, someone writes every word down. Those talks become a book that people in Maharashtra still read aloud together.
screen: `A TEMPLE BY A RIVER.` → `THE GITA, IN MARATHI.` → `SOMEONE WRITES IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: Tradition says this happened at Nevasa, and that the man writing was Sachchidananda. The book is the Jnaneshwari, and it isn't a translation in the usual sense. It walks through the Gita verse by verse and opens each one up with pictures from ordinary life. Take the Gita's line about the person of steady wisdom, who draws the senses in the way a tortoise draws in its limbs. Jnaneshwar lingers there, so a farmer or a potter could see it. The outcast boy of Paithan takes a teaching most people met in Sanskrit, a language few of his listeners had studied, and opens it in everyday Marathi. He even promises to make his words so sweet they'd win a wager against nectar: a bet that the language of the street can carry the deepest things. Hindus took that bet. It's a real conviction of the bhakti saints: God's word is for everyone, in their own tongue. It's why the Gita, the Ramayana and the saints' songs live on in Marathi, Tamil, Hindi, Bengali and many other languages, and why families read them aloud together. Varkari groups still read the Jnaneshwari aloud, and sing its words on pilgrimage. And all through the book, Jnaneshwar hands the credit to his teacher, Nivritti, who is also his older brother. The boldest claim about language, and the smallest about himself.
screen: `SPOKEN AT NEVASA, WRITTEN DOWN.` · `THE TORTOISE DRAWS IN ITS LIMBS.` · `SWEETER THAN NECTAR.` · then, large: `GOD'S WORD, IN YOUR OWN TONGUE.`

segments.voice: The Gita gives a picture you can try: the tortoise, drawing its limbs in. Sit, and one by one draw your attention in, from what you see, then what you hear, then the itch to check your phone, the way the tortoise pulls in each leg. Rest there a few breaths. Then think of who first put something holy into plain words for you, a parent, a grandparent, a teacher. If you pray, thank God for them; if not, say their name to yourself, once.
Jnaneshwar. The Marathi saint whose Jnaneshwari opened the Bhagavad Gita, verse by verse, in the language people spoke at home.

915.title: The wall that met the tiger
915.hook: a yogi rides in on a tiger, and the children ride out on a wall
915.carry: siddhis aren't holiness; the saint prays for all
915.howItsDone: Marathi-speaking devotees often recite the Pasayadan at the close of worship or gatherings, and pilgrims visit Jnaneshwar's samadhi shrine at Alandi, where his palanquin sets out on the Varkari pilgrimage to Pandharpur.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jnaneshwar again. He opened the Gita in Marathi, because God's word belongs in everyone's own tongue.
screen: `JNANESHWAR.` · `IN YOUR OWN TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Here comes a yogi, riding a tiger. In his hand, instead of a whip, a live snake. Behind him, a crowd of disciples. His name is Changdev, and tradition remembers him as a man of great yogic powers. He's heard about a young saint at Alandi, and he's coming to see him. At the other end of the road, Jnaneshwar, his brothers and his sister are sitting on a low wall in the sun. Someone runs up: he's coming.
screen: `A YOGI ON A TIGER.` → `A SNAKE FOR A WHIP.` → `CHILDREN ON A WALL.`

segments.voice: It starts with a letter that was never written. Changdev couldn't decide how to address Jnaneshwar. As an equal? A teacher? A boy? So he sent a blank sheet. Muktabai, the sister, is said to have read it and remarked that all his years of practice had left him blank. Then the tiger, the snake, the crowd. Jnaneshwar doesn't climb down. The story says he asks the wall to move, and the wall carries the four children down the road. Changdev, who had mastered a living tiger, sees children riding on stone, and the pride goes out of him. Tradition says he became a disciple, some tellings say of Muktabai herself. Here's the teaching under the joke. Hindu tradition has a word for powers like taming tigers: siddhis. The Yoga Sutras warn that such powers are obstacles on the way to samadhi. Stories like this one say it plainly: power isn't holiness. What holiness looks like comes at the close of the Jnaneshwari. Jnaneshwar asks God for a gift, a pasayadan, and it isn't for himself. He asks that the crookedness of the wicked fall away, that they come to love doing good, and that all beings become friends to one another. Tradition says that later, at Alandi, still a young man, he entered samadhi, a final meditation. So today, when you feel the pull to arrive on a tiger, at the temple or anywhere, the saint points to a plainer thing: humility, and a prayer that includes everyone.

segments.voice: Marathi-speaking devotees often close worship with the Pasayadan. Sit as you are, the way the children sat on the wall. Notice any wish to arrive impressively today, and let it soften. Then pray the way the Pasayadan does, for everyone: may the crookedness in people fall away; may all beings be friends. Wish it for the people you'll see, even one who's been hard on you. If you don't pray, simply wish each of them well, one by one.

916.title: The milk Vitthal drank
916.hook: a boy sets a bowl of milk before the god, and waits for him to drink
916.carry: naivedya: God receives what love offers
916.howItsDone: Varkari devotees sing abhangs, including Namdev's, in kirtan with cymbals, and the temple of Vitthal at Pandharpur keeps a step at its entrance named for Namdev.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-SIXTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jnaneshwar for the last time. The yogi on the tiger, the children on the willing wall: siddhis aren't holiness, and the saint prays for all.
screen: `JNANESHWAR.` · `THE SAINT PRAYS FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: A bowl of milk sits on the temple floor at Pandharpur, before the image of Vitthal, the dark god who stands on a brick with his hands on his hips. A small boy has carried it there. His father usually brings the offering, but he's away, so today the boy has been sent. He sets it down, folds his hands, and waits. The god doesn't move. The milk doesn't move. The boy keeps waiting. Nobody has told him that offerings are usually received unseen.
screen: `A BOWL OF MILK FOR VITTHAL.` → `A BOY SETS IT DOWN.` → `HE WAITS FOR THE GOD TO DRINK.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Namdev grew up in a family of tailors devoted to Vitthal, the form of Krishna worshiped at Pandharpur, whom devotees call Vithoba, and sometimes mother. As the story goes, the boy waits, and still the god doesn't drink. So he pleads. Why won't you take it? Some tellings say he cries; some say he threatens to break his own head on the stone floor if Vitthal refuses. And Vitthal, the story says, reaches out of the image and drinks the milk. All of it. The boy goes home with an empty bowl, and nobody believes him. It's funny, and it's also about something Hindus do every day. It's called naivedya: food is offered to God first, at the home shrine or in the temple, before anyone eats. Devotees trust that God receives it all the same, and what comes back is prasad, food made holy by being offered, shared with everyone. Namdev's story is the one where a child got to see it received. He takes Vitthal at his word, the way a child takes anyone at their word, and the story rewards him instead of correcting him. Namdev grows up to be a singer. His songs, called abhangs, talk to Vitthal like someone in the same room: pleading, teasing, longing. Varkaris still sing them in kirtan, call and response, with cymbals keeping the beat.
screen: `A FAMILY OF TAILORS, DEVOTED TO VITTHAL.` · `WHY WON'T YOU TAKE IT?` · `VITTHAL DRINKS THE MILK.` · then, large: `NAIVEDYA: OFFERED FIRST, RECEIVED.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, as if holding a small bowl, and think of something simple you'll eat or drink today. Before you do, you'll hold it up for a moment and offer it, the way the boy did, as if it will really be received; then eat it as prasad. If you pray, offer it to God, by Vitthal's name or any name you already use. If you don't, offer thanks to whoever grew it or made it.
Namdev. The tailor's son of the Marathi saint tradition, who, the story says, waited until Vitthal drank the milk, and grew up singing abhangs.

917.title: Nowhere to put the feet
917.hook: a potter taps each saint's head, and an old man won't keep his feet off the linga
917.carry: nowhere to put the feet where God is not
917.howItsDone: The stories of Gora the potter and Visoba Khechar belong to the Varkari tradition of Maharashtra, whose members sing the songs of Namdev and the other saints of Pandharpur in praise of Vitthal.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-SEVENTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Namdev, the boy who set a bowl of milk before Vitthal and waited until, the story says, the god drank it. Naivedya: God receives what love offers.
screen: `NAMDEV.` · `GOD RECEIVES WHAT LOVE OFFERS.`

segments.voice: A potter walks down a row of seated saints, holding the flat wooden paddle he uses on pots. He taps a pot and listens: fired all the way through, or still soft inside? The story says Jnaneshwar asked him, Gora the potter, to test the devotees gathered there. So Gora taps each head. Each saint sits quietly and takes it. Then he reaches Namdev, and Namdev bristles, and says so. Gora listens, and tells the whole room: this pot is still half-baked.
screen: `GORA THE POTTER.` → `HE TAPS EACH HEAD.` → `THIS POT IS HALF-BAKED.`

segments.voice: That stung, because Namdev's love for Vitthal was real. So he runs to Vitthal to complain. And Vitthal, in the story, takes the potter's side. You have love, he says. What you don't have yet is a teacher. Go and find Visoba Khechar. Namdev finds the old man asleep in a Shiva temple, his feet resting on the linga, the stone that stands for Shiva. Shocked, Namdev wakes him. I'm old and tired. Lift my feet, please, and set them down somewhere God is not. Namdev moves them. A linga rises up under them. He moves them again. Another. Wherever the feet come down, Shiva is already there. At last Namdev sets them in his own lap, and he understands: there is nowhere to put the feet, because there is nowhere without God. It's one of Hinduism's oldest teachings: the Isha Upanishad opens by saying that all this, whatever moves in the world, is pervaded by the Lord. So what was wrong with the pot? Not too little devotion. Devotion with walls around it, so fond of God in one image, in one town, that it couldn't see him anywhere else. Hindus take care not to point their feet at a shrine, out of respect. Visoba isn't mocking that respect. He's showing where it leads: if God is everywhere, every place deserves it. All week, a mango, a song, a buffalo, a wall, a bowl of milk: wherever the saints looked, God was already there.
screen: `A POTTER CALLS HIM HALF-BAKED.` · `VITTHAL SAYS: FIND A TEACHER.` · `FEET ON THE LINGA.` · then, large: `NOWHERE TO PUT THE FEET.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ordinary place you'll be later: a bus seat, a sink full of dishes, a waiting room. Set your attention down there gently, the way Namdev set down those tired feet, and ask: what if God is already here too? If you pray, you can hold that place before God. If you don't, simply plan to treat that place, for one moment, with the care you'd give a shrine.
Namdev. The poet-saint of Pandharpur, called half-baked by a potter, who learned from Visoba Khechar that there's nowhere to put the feet where God is not.
